Section 12.2

```{r}
set.seed(1119)
library(tidyverse)
library(here) 

pokemon <- read_csv(here("data", "pokemon_full.csv")) |>
  filter(Type %in% c("Steel", "Dark", "Fire", "Ice")) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ (.x - min(.x)) /
                                 (max(.x) - min(.x)))) 
## for any numeric variable in the data set (where(is.numeric))
## apply the formula x - min(x) / (max(x) - min(x))
```

```{r}
train_sample <- pokemon |>
  slice_sample(n = 75)

test_sample <- anti_join(pokemon, train_sample)

library(GGally)
ggpairs(data = train_sample, columns = c(4, 5, 6, 3))
```

for association with type, we want to look at the last column of boxplots.

the diagonal shows density plots (smoothed histograms) for quantitative variables and a bar plot for categorical variables.

definitely defense (since, on average, steel type pokemon have higher defense than the other three types), but attack and hp also look like they are mildly associated with type. So, all three might be good to include initially!

```{r}
ggpairs(data = train_sample, columns = c(7, 8, 9, 3))
```

```{r}
library(kknn)

knn_mod <- kknn(Type ~ Attack + Defense + Speed, train = train_sample,
                test = test_sample, k = 9)
knn_mod
## errors because Type must be <fct>, not <chr>

set.seed(1119)

pokemon <- read_csv(here("data", "pokemon_full.csv")) |>
  filter(Type %in% c("Steel", "Dark", "Fire", "Ice")) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ (.x - min(.x)) /
                                 (max(.x) - min(.x)))) |>
  mutate(Type = as.factor(Type))
## now Type is a factor!

train_sample <- pokemon |>
  slice_sample(n = 75)

test_sample <- anti_join(pokemon, train_sample)

knn_mod <- kknn(Type ~ Attack + Defense + Speed, train = train_sample,
                test = test_sample, k = 9)
## works now since Type is a factor!
knn_mod

knn_mod$fitted.values
## a vector of predicted classes for all of the pokemon in
## the test sample
```

## Section 12.3: Evaluating the Model

```{r}
table(knn_mod$fitted.values, test_sample$Type) 
```

Exercise 5.

__Classification Rate__: number of correct classifications divided by the total number in the test sample.

```{r}
(2 + 12 + 1 + 5) / 45
## classification rate is 0.444

tab <- table(knn_mod$fitted.values, test_sample$Type) 
sum(diag(tab)) / sum(tab)
```

Exercise 7.

```{r}
## baseline classification rate is a classification rate from just
## classifying every observation in the test sample as the most
## common level found in the training sample.

train_sample
test_sample

## 1. use the training sample to figure out the most common type.
train_sample |> group_by(Type) |>
  summarise(n = n()) |>
  arrange(desc(n))

## most common type in the training sample is Fire

## 2. use the test sample to calculate the proportion of pokemon
## that match the most common type in the training sample.
test_sample |>
  group_by(Type) |>
  summarise(n_type = n()) |>
  ungroup() |>
  summarise(prop = 16 / sum(n_type))

## slightly more reproducible
test_sample |>
  mutate(fire_ind = if_else(Type == "Fire",
                            true = 1, 
                            false = 0)) |>
  relocate(fire_ind) |> ## select(fire_ind, everything())
  summarise(prop_fire = mean(fire_ind))
```

Exercise 8.

smaller $k$ means that you are using only the pokemon that are most similar to a particular test pokemon when classifying. But, the disadvantage of making $k$ too small is that there might be a lot of variability if, for instance, $k$ is only 1 or 2. This is what's called the "bias-variance trade-off."

Class Exercises

```{r}
library(tidyverse)

pokemon <- read_csv(here::here("data/pokemon_full.csv")) |>
  mutate(Type = as.factor(Type))
set.seed(1119)

## scale the quantitative predictors
pokemon_scaled <- pokemon |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ (.x - min(.x)) /
                  (max(.x) - min(.x))))

train_sample <- pokemon_scaled |>
  slice_sample(n = 550)
test_sample <- anti_join(pokemon_scaled, train_sample)

library(kknn)

knn_mod <- kknn(Type ~ HP + Attack + Defense + Speed + SpAtk + SpDef + height + weight,
                train = train_sample, test = test_sample, k = 9)
knn_mod

tab <- table(knn_mod$fitted.values, test_sample$Type)
sum(diag(tab)) / sum(tab)
```

```{r}
get_class_rate <- function(k_val) {
  knn_mod <- kknn(Type ~ HP + Attack + Defense + Speed + SpAtk + SpDef + height + weight,
                  train = train_sample, test = test_sample, k = k_val)
  
  tab <- table(knn_mod$fitted.values, test_sample$Type)
  class_rate <- sum(diag(tab)) / sum(tab)
  
  return(class_rate)
}
get_class_rate(k_val = 30)

kvec <- 1:60
class_rates <- map_dbl(kvec, get_class_rate)

class_df <- tibble(kvec, class_rates)
class_df

## make a line plot fo the classifications rate
## write code to figure out which k value has the maximum classification
## rate.
ggplot(data = class_df, aes(x = kvec, y = class_rates)) +
  geom_line()
class_df |> filter(class_rates == max(class_rates))
```
